THE CENTRAL QUESTION

What does the system reward—and what does it leave unmeasured?

READ THIS FIRST

Hold two truths
at the same time.

Medicines can deliver enormous public benefit. Pharmaceutical companies can also commit serious misconduct. Neither statement cancels the other. The useful question is how to preserve the first while making the second harder, less profitable and easier to detect.

This is an independent reconstruction of the subject, not a new skin over the original BigPharma database. It follows a medicine from discovery to the patient, examines a deliberately selected set of documented cases, and asks what better rules would actually change.

01 / THE SYSTEM

A medicine is more
than a molecule.

Every stage creates value. Every stage also creates an opportunity to move risk onto somebody else.

The innovation bargain

Research requires time, expertise, capital and willingness to fail. Patents and regulatory exclusivity can allow a successful product to earn returns before competition arrives. That is the policy bargain: temporary protection in exchange for innovation and, eventually, wider access.

But a reward for selling a product is not automatically a reward for meeting the greatest health need. A market can be very good at attracting capital and still be poor at serving people with little purchasing power. Evaluating the bargain requires asking what was developed, how much better it is, who helped pay for the science, and who can obtain the result.

Read the economics →

Follow the decision rights

The sponsor can influence the research question, comparator, endpoints and publication plan. Regulators decide whether evidence meets a legal threshold. Purchasers and insurers decide what they will pay for. Prescribers and patients make decisions inside those constraints.

“Big pharma” is therefore a useful shorthand but an incomplete map. Universities, investors, journals, contract research organisations, regulators, insurers, pharmacy benefit managers and governments also shape the outcome. A serious investigation identifies which actor controlled the decision.

Follow the price chain →
02 / THE EVIDENCE

A good headline
is not a full result.

Before asking whether a finding is persuasive, ask what was measured, who was studied, and what is missing.

INTERACTIVE EXPLAINER / HYPOTHETICAL DATA

Same relative benefit.
Very different stakes.

A treatment reduces the relative risk of an event. Change the starting risk to see what that means in a group of 1,000 people over the same fixed follow-up period.

Teaching model, not a forecast for any medicine. It assumes a constant relative effect and omits uncertainty, harms and competing risks.

Without treatment100 / 1,000
With treatment75 / 1,000
25fewer events per 1,000
40treated for one event prevented*

*Number needed to treat, rounded up, over the hypothetical follow-up. Formula: 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction.

A

The denominator

Relative effects need a baseline risk and a time horizon. An outcome that changes from 2 in 100 to 1 in 100 is a 50% relative reduction, but one fewer event per 100 people. Neither description is wrong; one alone is incomplete.

B

The comparison

A treatment can beat placebo without being better than the best existing option. Check the comparator, dose, patient group and follow-up. A useful result answers a real treatment decision, not just the easiest question to win.

C

The endpoint

A laboratory measurement may be faster to study than whether people live longer or feel better. A surrogate can be informative, but an improvement in the marker does not itself establish a patient-important benefit.

D

The missing record

A study that is never reported cannot contribute normally to a treatment decision. Compare the trial registration, protocol and published report. Ask whether the primary outcome, analysis population or reporting plan changed.

Funding is a reason to examine a study, not a shortcut to rejecting it.

Study design, preregistration, independent replication, access to data and the full body of evidence matter more than a sponsor label alone. Transparency failures also occur in publicly funded research.

03 / THE CASEBOOK

Read the finding.
Then read the fine print.

A selected record of enforcement, not a league table of evil. The legal outcome is part of the story.

Criminal outcomeCivil resolution / court findingDeferred prosecution
No cases match these filters.

Why there is no giant “total fines” counter

A criminal fine, a civil settlement, a forfeiture order and a bankruptcy claim are different things. Announced liabilities may overlap or be discharged, credited or paid over time. Adding them can make an impressive number without producing a defensible one. Amounts here retain their original currency, nominal value, date and legal context. They are not a measure of cash collected or patient harm.

04 / PRICE & POWER

There is no single
“price of a drug.”

List price, net price, reimbursement and out-of-pocket cost answer different questions. Mixing them can hide who benefits.

List price

A published starting price. It does not reveal every rebate or discount.

03 / PATIENT

Personal cost

Insurance rules, co-payments, deductibles and eligibility shape the bill.

Conceptual map, not a transaction model. The route differs by country and payer; some payments run back through the chain.

The middle of the chain matters

In its January 2025 interim report, FTC staff examined 51 specialty generic drugs in data from the three largest US pharmacy benefit managers. Affiliated pharmacies generated more than $7.3 billion in dispensing revenue above estimated acquisition costs during 2017–2022.

That is a benchmark comparison for a particular dataset—not an industry-wide profit estimate or a criminal judgment. It shows why investigating manufacturers alone misses part of the pricing system.

FTC staff report and scope →

A discount needs a denominator

When CMS announced the first ten negotiated Medicare drug prices in August 2024, it estimated that applying them to 2023 use would have reduced net spending by about 22%, or $6 billion. The much larger 38–79% discounts were comparisons with list prices.

These are different comparisons. The $6 billion figure was a retrospective modelling estimate, not observed savings from 2026. Neither percentage predicts what a particular person pays.

CMS announcement and definitions →
THE OFTEN-MISSED FAILURE

Some medicines can be too cheap
to be reliably supplied.

Monopoly pricing and shortages are not opposites that cancel each other out. Different parts of the market can fail differently. A fragile supply chain for an older medicine can coexist with high prices for a protected new one. Policy should reward reliable quality and supply as well as competition.

Read the FDA shortage analysis ↗
05 / WHAT GETS BUILT

Commercial value
is not health value.

The absence of a medicine can be as important as the behaviour of a company selling one.

WHO PIPELINE SNAPSHOT · DEC 202312/32

antibiotics targeting priority pathogens met WHO's innovation criteria.

Published June 2024 ↗

The antibiotic paradox

We want effective antibiotics available when they are needed—and used sparingly enough to preserve their effectiveness. That creates a tension with a business model based on maximising sales volume.

WHO's 2024 analysis found that only 12 of 32 antibiotics in development against priority-pathogen infections met its innovation criteria. Only four of those 12 were active against at least one pathogen in the highest-priority category. Pipeline size alone is therefore a poor measure of whether unmet need is being addressed.

This is a dated research snapshot, not the current count of approved antibiotics. The overall 97-product clinical pipeline included non-traditional antibacterials and broader targets.

Reward availability, not just volume

One policy direction is to pay for access to an effective antibiotic while separating some of the reward from the number of doses sold. Another is to share early research costs. These approaches still need conditions: demonstrated clinical value, stewardship, dependable manufacturing and access in the places carrying the burden.

Editorial proposal, not a claim that any particular funding scheme has already solved the problem.

Approval is only one milestone

A product that exists but cannot be diagnosed for, supplied, afforded or administered is not an accessible treatment. Infrastructure, procurement and distribution are part of the innovation story. Counting approvals is easier than measuring how many people can actually benefit.

WHO on innovation and equitable access →
06 / THE AUSTRALIAN LENS

Two gates.
Two different questions.

Being allowed to sell a medicine and having it subsidised are separate decisions. Understanding that distinction changes the debate.

GATE 01 / TGA

Can it be supplied?

The Therapeutic Goods Administration evaluates prescription medicines for quality, safety and efficacy. Its assessment concerns a particular product and use; registration is not a promise of zero risk.

The regulatory gate ↗
GATE 02 / PBAC → PBS

Should it be subsidised?

The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee considers comparative effectiveness, safety and cost-effectiveness when making PBS recommendations. A favourable recommendation is a key step, not the whole pricing and listing process.

The subsidy gate ↗

Why “available overseas” is incomplete

Countries can consider different submissions, comparators, evidence and prices. A difference in access is a reason to inspect the decision, not proof that one agency is either captured or indifferent. Look for the indication, population and terms of the proposed subsidy.

A company may seek a price that a public purchaser considers poor value compared with other uses of the health budget. Equally, delayed access can matter greatly to people with few alternatives. The trade-off should be made explicit.

How to investigate a medicine here

  1. Identify it precisely. Use the active ingredient, strength and intended use, not only the brand.
  2. Read the Australian product information. Check the indication, warnings and study population.
  3. Look at the PBS restriction. Eligibility can be narrower than the registered indication.
  4. Read the PBAC public summary. Look for the comparator, uncertainty and economic reasoning.
  5. Bring the evidence to a clinician or pharmacist. A company case file cannot decide an individual's treatment.
07 / ACCOUNTABILITY

Better rules need
better scoreboards.

Counting fines or approvals is not enough. These are editorial tests for whether a reform is working—not a claim that improvement has already occurred.

THE EDITORIAL JUDGMENT

Trust should be earned
by a system you can inspect.

A useful medicine does not excuse dishonest promotion. A corporate settlement does not establish that every product is ineffective. The strongest response to both complacency and blanket distrust is an inspectable record: what was promised, what was tested, what was found, what was paid and what changed.

Demand more than a dramatic fine. Demand that negative results remain visible, competing treatments receive a fair comparison, access is measured beyond launch, and sanctions change the incentives of the people making decisions.

08 / THE OPEN NOTEBOOK

Inspect the evidence.
Keep the caveats.

The research behind the investigation, with dated findings and limits. Case-specific legal sources are also linked inside each case file.

Selection

This is a curated explanatory sample, weighted toward US enforcement because its primary records are accessible. It is not a census, a representative prevalence study, a safety ranking, or a comparison adjusted for company size.

Attribution

Cases identify the company or entity involved at the time. A subsidiary's plea is not silently relabelled as a parent's conviction. Civil allegations, settlements, deferred prosecutions and court findings receive different labels.

Time & money

Event dates and source dates are shown separately where needed. Historical announcements describe their own time. Amounts are nominal US dollars unless otherwise stated; they are not added into a grand total.

What remains uncertain

Public records rarely establish all downstream health effects or whether an intervention deterred future misconduct. Official releases are primary evidence of government actions, not neutral adjudications of every allegation.

Research notes

A short glossary
Absolute risk reduction
The difference between event probabilities in two groups over the same period.
Civil settlement
An agreement resolving civil claims; it may expressly avoid admitting liability.
Deferred prosecution agreement
A criminal resolution that defers prosecution subject to conditions. It is not itself a trial conviction.
Exclusivity
A regulatory protection against certain competing approvals; legally distinct from a patent.
Indication
The disease, patient group or use for which a medicine is intended or authorised.
Off-label use
Use outside an approved indication or other label conditions. Clinical prescribing and unlawful promotional conduct are different questions.
Surrogate endpoint
A measurement used in place of a direct outcome such as survival, symptoms or function.
Net price
A price after specified rebates or discounts. Always ask which adjustments are included.
A record of companies is not a treatment recommendation.

Do not stop or change a prescribed medicine because of a case on this site. Discuss the evidence, benefits, harms and alternatives with your clinician or pharmacist.
